target_customer: Drivers with spare seats and riders on long-distance trips
problem: Long-distance travelers pay a lot and drivers with empty seats have no trusted way to share costs.
business_model: marketplace take rate on shared ride costs

founders.name: Kalvin Wang
founders.background_notes: Created BurningManRides.com, the origin of Ridejoy, per TechCrunch coverage.

founders.name: Jason Shen
education: Stanford, 2009 (degree not stated; YC founder bio)
founders.background_notes: Wrote the Ridejoy lessons learned post.

founders.name: Randy Pang
founders.background_notes: Named co-founder in Shen's post (the three were roommates).

exit.reason: Founders concluded long-distance carpooling would not reach venture scale; they returned about half the seed round to investors.

competitors.name: Zimride
competitors.what: Carpooling and ridesharing network started at universities

competitors.name: Craigslist rideshare section
competitors.what: Classified listings that were Ridejoy's biggest source of users

technical_complexity.rationale: A marketplace with trip search, messaging, payments and an iPhone app (August 2012) is standard engineering for a small team.

defensibility.rationale: Supply and demand came largely from Craigslist and the product was easy to copy; economics gave drivers little reason to stay.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: Per Shen, Craigslist sent cease-and-desist letters in fall 2012 against his main user source; Zimride sold its carpooling business in 2013.

market_need_then: BurningManRides.com drew about 1,600 people and over 1,200 posted rides in 2011 (TechCrunch coverage), showing event driven demand; later growth did not support full time driver earnings.

branding.domain_note: Used ridejoy.com; per Shen the domain lapsed in April 2015 after the team forgot to renew, and it is now used by an unrelated horse travel site.

identity.logo: not described in any source found
identity.voice_and_tone: Friendly, community oriented: a marketplace of 'friendly people sharing rides'.

branding.brand_signature: BurningManRides.com, the Burning Man ride board that Ridejoy grew from.
branding.community_and_virality: The Burning Man ride board drew press such as Laughing Squid and TechCrunch in 2011 and 2012.

brand_strength.rationale: Warm name and a memorable event origin earned press, but the brand was not enough to fix marketplace economics.

pivots.from: Reloveit (the idea originally applied to YC with)

outcome_analysis: Ridejoy grew from a Burning Man ride board into a long-distance carpooling marketplace and raised a $1.3M seed in February 2012, but drivers earned too little to commit full time and its main acquisition channel, Craigslist, pushed back in fall 2012. After about 18 months and six months of searching for a new idea, the team returned about half the seed and shut down in 2013.
notes: Shutdown date conflicts: YC says early 2013, GigaOM dated 2013-12-17 reports Ridejoy will shut down, and Shen's post says operations ended in 2013; 2013-12 follows GigaOM. The Craigslist cease-and-desist claim rests on Shen's post; a separate search found no corroboration. Competitor sources are dated June 2012, about ten months after the batch, so they exceed the usual window; no earlier dated source was found. The YC deal ($20K) is recorded as stage other because Shen's post reports it. Failure factors are my judgment from Shen's own account. The Craigslist letter date is stated as fall 2012 in the post, not a precise date.
